transcript: Chapter 9. He stopped singing, and then he stopped walking, and the thing in the ditch stayed stopped. Jab stood in the middle of the road and looked at it. It was thirty feet away and a little below him, down on the slumped shoulder where the ditch began, and it was long in the body and short in the leg in the color of wet ash. The head was a heavy wedge carried low. That was all he could see, and he could only see that much because the amber line on his fist put a wash of light out to about there and no further, and because the animal had a way of taking the light that was wrong. It did not shine, and it did not go dull. The light came off its back with a shiver in it, the way air shivers over a hot stone, except that the shiver was in the animal and not in the air. His whole body knew before he did. His arms had gone cold to the elbow. Wolf, said the part of him that had grown up four hundred miles north of here, and then, immediately, in his father's voice, no it isn't. He had seen wolves. Wolves in the home valley did not come to a person on a road, and if they did, they came apologizing, sideways with their tails and their ears making a speech about it the whole time. This one was not making a speech. It stood in the ditch side onto him, absolutely still, from lope to stillness with nothing in between, and it did not look at him so much as it stood there being aimed at him. Jab, said Tonk, behind his ear. There's a dog. I see it. It's not moving. I know. Jab did the thing he knew. There was no other thing to do, so he did the one from home, and it was not a stupid thing to do. He made himself big. He put his shoulders back and raised the blade up and out so the light went wide, and he took two whole steps forward, and he shouted at it. The flat-carrying bark his ant on the smoking side used on the dogs at the racks, a noise with no word in it at all. The noise that had turned every animal he had met in seventeen years. It did not turn. It did not flinch or lift its head, or shift its weight. Nothing at all happened to it, and a distance up the ditch behind it something else came up out of the black water and stood still as well. Then a third on the other side of the road. Right, said Jab. His voice came out of him very level and did not feel like his. Right. All right. He started walking. They kept station with him. That was the part he could not get his mind around, and it was the part that told him more than anything else on that road. They did not rush, and they did not hang back. He walked, and they went along the ditches at exactly his pace. The near one on the left and two more strung out on the right, loose, unhurried, never bunching. And when he sped up, they were already going faster, and when he stopped, they stopped a half-second later. He counted. He could not stop counting. It was the thing his head did when it had nothing better. Three, then four. Then a fifth came up out of the ditch behind him, which he only knew because Tonk said in a small, flat voice, there's one at the back. And Jab said, I know, and did not turn round. And it was a lie in both directions because he had not known, and he wanted very badly to turn round. Down the road there were lamps. He had been walking toward them for ten minutes and had not let himself think about them. There was a knot of yellow light a quarter mile ahead where the road went into a long, shallow dip, not station light, not the flat white lamp on its pole, but the moving orange of real flame, four or five of them, low down in shapes going about in front of them. People. A cart or a barrow. Somebody with a lamp on a pole walking a line and stopping. A quarter mile. Four hundred paces. At the pace he could make with the frame on, five minutes. The nearest hound came up out of the ditch onto the shoulder. It did it in one movement, without hurrying. And now it was on the roadbed with him, twenty feet off his left elbow going along at his speed. And in the amber light he could see the whole length of it, and it was as long as he was tall. Five minutes was too long. He knew that the way he had known, standing on a gravel bench above a flooded creek, that the downstream detour was two and a half days he did not have. It was not a feeling. It was arithmetic, tick. And he had been doing arithmetic on his feet for sixteen days. He could not run. With the frame loaded he could make, at a shambling, terrified trot, perhaps half again his walking speed, for about a hundred paces, and then he would go down. He had gone down on flat ground in daylight with nothing chasing him. He could not fight like this. He had a blade on his right fist and a hundred and some pounds of brother strapped to his back and hips, and a rail that ran out past his own width on the right so that he could not turn quickly to that side without swinging his brother's broken leg through the air. He could not get out of the belt with one hand. He could not put his back against anything, because his back was where Tonk was. He could not do both. That was the whole of it, and it arrived in him complete, in one piece, with no argument attached. You cannot carry him and stand in front of him at the same time. So he looked for the corner. The road went down into its dip, and the dip was a bad place, and even at a walk with five animals pacing him, he could see it was a bad place. The maid's surface broke up into slabs, tilted, with black water standing in the joints. The shoulders had slumped down into the ditches on both sides, so that the road stopped having edges and started having slopes. And at the bottom of the dip, something went under the road. He could hear it before he reached it, water running in a pipe, and where it went under, the old builders had put in stone. There was a squared head of masonry at the lip of the culvert on the west side. A wing wall two courses higher than the shoulder, running back from the road edge into the bank at a right angle, with a flat coping on top at about the height of his chest. The angle it made with the roadbed was a little hollow of dead grass about four feet across, floored with broken stone, walled on two sides. Two sides. Not four. Two was what there was. Tonk, he said. Listen to me and don't ask me anything yet. Is it the dogs? Yes. I'm going to put you down. No. Yes. He was already going to his knees beside the wall, and the whole of it had begun to happen very fast and very slowly at once. You're going in the corner, and I'm going to stand in front of you, and I can't do that with you on my back. That's the whole reason. There isn't another one. He got the belt buckle. It took two hands, and it took four seconds, and he spent every one of those four seconds with his head up, looking over the coping, at the shapes standing in the road behind him doing nothing at all. They were doing nothing at all. That was what they had been doing for ten minutes. They had had ten minutes to come at him on open road, and they had not, and somewhere under the fear, a small cold part of Jab's mind filed that and said, they're not hunting you yet. They're counting. Getting a child with a broken leg out of a carrying frame took nine minutes if you did it properly. He did it in about 90 seconds, and he did it wrong, and it was the worst thing he had ever done to his brother. He had to take the ankle strap and the thigh strap and the chest band in an order that did not matter anymore, and he had to take the leg off the rail without the forearm under the calf and the elbow under the knee, because he had one hand for that and the other was holding the frame off the boy while it tipped. The rail dragged. The leg went through an angle it had not gone through since the gravel bar, and Tonk screamed, the raw full scream. The one jab had heard twice in his life and would hear in his sleep for the rest of it, and kept screaming while Jab got both arms under him and lifted him bodily off the ground and put him down in the angle of the wall on the dead grass. I know. I know, I know. He got the hideout from under the frame's cover and got it round him. He got the blanket. He wedged the frame itself on its side across the roadside of the hollow lattice outward, which was not a wall, but was a thing that would have to be come over or come round. That left the south side open, four feet of dead grass between the end of the frame and the bank, and nothing in it at all. Then he took the twelve-foot cord off his own left wrist, where it had been tied every night for six days, and put the end of it into his brother's fist and closed the fingers over it. Cord, he said. Tonk was sobbing and could not talk. Cord. Look at it. You pull that and I'm there. That's all it's ever meant and it means it now. He got the wooden fish off the stone where it had fallen and put it into the other hand, and Tonk's fingers closed on it so hard the knuckles went white. Now. Here's your job, Jab, and it's a real one. I don't want a job. There's people down the road with lamps. Four hundred paces. When you see them coming, you shout. And you shout the whole time and you don't stop. And don't you dare stop because you think I'm busy. Jab put his forehead against his brother's forehead for exactly as long as he could afford, which was one second. Arms in. Eyes wherever you like. Then he stood up in front of the corner with the cord's other end tied round nothing at all, and turned round, and brought the light back up along the edge of the blade. Grip outward, amber, thin. The gutter at the belly. One breath of it. Guttering and catching. Then the whole edge lit and the hook at the end. There were five of them on the road and they were much closer than they had been. They had come up while he was on his knees. Of course they had. He had spent ninety seconds facing a wall with his hands full, and they had spent it moving, and now the nearest was eighteen feet away on the crown of the road and the rest were spread out behind and beside it in a loose fan that had the culvert head at the middle of it. None of them was looking at him. They were all looking past him at the corner, at the small shape in the dark behind his legs, and Jab understood with total clarity that they had not been counting him at all. They had been counting the thing he was carrying. They had been counting it for two miles, up a road, by the smell of an open wound and a fever at the top of its arc. Something happened in his chest that was not fear, although the fear was still there underneath it, running. No, he said. He stepped forward off the corner. That was the first thing he got wrong, and it was a reasonable thing to get wrong, and it nearly finished both of them. Here was his reasoning, and it had four years of use behind it. The metal was a tool. Dark. It was a heavy blunt wedge that would break a rope and split a log and take three strokes to get through the wet outside of a standing dead spruce. Lit. It went through green willow like nothing at all, and had once opened a jam that would have taken six people a day. Lit was what made it dangerous. Therefore, when a dangerous thing came at him, he should be the most dangerous he could possibly be, and he should be that out in front where it could be seen. So he lit it wide and high, and he took two steps out onto the road and put himself between the fan and the corner with the light up in front of him. And the whole fan came off him like water off a plate. It was not a retreat. That was what took him so long to understand, standing there with his blade out and his heart going. They did not back away, and they did not break. They slid the nearest one first, and then the rest, all of them at the same speed. The way a flock of birds turns without anybody deciding. Round to his right, away from the lit edge, out along the fan toward the open road and the top of the ditch. Toward the south side. Toward the four feet of dead grass, the frame was not across. Jab went after it. There was no thought in it. He turned and went right, with the blade out, and the fan simply went further right, and then the near one on the far end of the arc, the one he had stopped watching because his eyes were full of the ones in front of him, put its head down and came. It came fast and low and absolutely silent, and it did not come at Jab. It went for the south side. He got there because of the rail, not because of anything he did. He had spun to follow the fan, and the frame was lying on its side in front of the corner with the curved ash rail standing up off it, and he took the rail across the shin, and falling forward put him four feet further right than any decision of his would have got him. And he came down on his left hand and one knee in the open grass with the lit blade held out sideways across his own body. The hound went on to it. He felt the whole event through the bones of his arm. Not a cut. A collision. The shoulder of something heavy running onto a held edge at speed, and the edge going in and the weight coming through after it. His arm folded. His elbow hit the stone. The blade came out somewhere and the hound went past him and into the frame and through it, through it, splitting the ash lattice with a crack like a shot. And Tonk shrieked in the corner. Jab got his feet under him with no memory of deciding to- The hound was turning in the four feet of space between the broken frame and the bank, turning badly, dragging its near foreleg, and its head was already coming round toward the corner and the small noise in it. He went over it. He did not have a technique. He had four years of putting a heavy blade through wet wood at awkward angles from bad footing, which was, it turned out, not nothing. He got his left hand into the scruff of the thing. It was like taking hold of a sack of hot sand that was moving, and put his weight onto it and drove the lit edge down and in behind the shoulder, using the belly of the shape, the fat part. The part his father had explained to him on a gravel bar. It's for when you can't get behind a thing and you have to cut it from the side. It came apart. Not the way a deer came apart. It came apart all at once and from everywhere, the entire animal letting go of being an animal. And what had been a hundred and something pounds of something under his hands was a gray blowing weight of ash that went through his fingers and up his sleeves and into his mouth and eyes, and Jab knelt in the gap in a cloud of it. Coughing, retching with the blade still lit in his fist. Jab. Here. He could not see. I'm here. I'm here. Don't move. He got one eye clear with the back of his wrist and dragged himself backward out of the open grass, into the angle, until his shoulder found stone. There were four hounds standing on the road, spread across the crown at the lip of the dip, absolutely still, side on, heads low. They had not moved at all. Not one of them had come in behind the first. They had stood there and watched the thing happen from twenty feet away. And now they were doing the other thing. The stillness. The thing the first one had done in the ditch at thirty feet, and he had thought was hesitation. And behind them, out at the edge of the amber, a fifth one that he had lost the count of, stood on the shoulder with its head up. His left forearm had a hole in it. He noticed that in the flat way you notice a thing during, rather than after. There was a warm, wet weight in the sleeve, and his fingers had gone slow. The scruff. It had got its head round while he had hold of it. He had not felt any of it happen. His right hand was still holding the blade and the light was still on, and the light was costing him, and he could feel exactly what it was costing, which was the last of a bucket that had been nearly empty since a night in the snow. He got up and put himself in the open south side. That was the whole of the plan, and it took him about a second to arrive at. And it was the only ground on the road that mattered, four feet of dead grass with the bank at his left shoulder, the broken frame at his right, and his brother in the angle of the wall behind his heels. He stood in it with the blade lit, and his left arm hanging, and four hounds standing out on the crown of the road in front of him, and he had no idea at all what to do next. Tonk, are you in one piece? It broke the frame. Are you in one piece? Yes. Good. Shout now. What? The people, said Jab. The lamps. Shout for them. Shout now and don't stop. And his brother, four years old, lying on broken stone in the angle of a culvert wall with a wooden fish in one fist and a cord in the other, filled his lungs and shouted a high, cracked, furious noise that went out down a straight road under a black sky and did not sound like a boy at all. The four hounds did not move. And then from somewhere down the road in the dark, not from the lamps, from much nearer than the lamps, off the shoulder where there was nothing to see at all, a girl's voice came back. It was flat and hard and it was not shouting at him. It was shouting at somebody a long way behind her, and every word of it arrived clean along the cold still air of the roadbed. That's the light. That's where they've gone. Five went past me up the west ditch four minutes ago and I said so twice.
